conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, everything is confidential, and we can pause any time. When you’re ready, we’ll go through each question together so we can figure out the best support for you.

To start: overall, in the past week, have you found yourself still able to enjoy things the way you used to, or has that felt harder lately?

[eyes down, rocking slightly in the chair]

It’s… harder. I still smile when my little guy grabs my finger or when my sister brought over that dumb show we like, but the spark is dimmer—like I’m watching myself enjoy stuff from behind a pane of glass. Most things feel flat, like I’m just going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile that fades quickly]

Yeah… I guess I laugh sometimes—like when my husband made that silly face changing her diaper—but it feels kind of forced. The laughter doesn’t last, and I don’t really feel it in my chest the way I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[twisting the edge of the baby blanket in my lap]

Not really… I mean, I tell myself I *should* look forward to coffee with my friend tomorrow, but mostly I feel dread that I’ll have to pretend everything’s fine. Even little things—like taking the baby for a walk—just feel like tasks I have to get through, not something I actually anticipate enjoying.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[sighs, voice drops]

Yeah... pretty much every day. Yesterday she wouldn't nap and I kept thinking it was because I missed her sleepy-cues or I drank that extra cup of coffee. If she fusses, my brain jumps straight to "I'm doing something wrong." Even when my partner says it’s normal baby stuff, I still feel like I’m failing her somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[hugging the baby blanket tighter]

All the time. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly picture her choking—even though she’s latched fine—then I can’t shake the image. Or I’ll lie awake imagining the crib slats somehow smothering her. I *know* it’s unlikely, but the fear just loops in my head until I have to check the monitor again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breath catches]

Yeah... it hits out of nowhere. Last night I was folding her onesies and suddenly my heart started racing, like something awful was about to happen. No trigger—just this wave of panic that maybe I’ll drop her, or that the house isn’t safe. It passes, but those minutes feel endless.
Things have been getting on top of me

[quiet laugh, eyes glassy]

Most days, yeah. I’ll finally get her down for a nap and the sink’s piled with bottles, the laundry’s overflowing, and I think, “I can’t breathe.” Sometimes I just sit on the floor while she cries for a minute because I don’t know which thing to tackle first.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[rubbing my temples]

That’s been almost every night this week. I lie there listening for her breathing, running through everything I might’ve messed up, and sleep just… won’t come. Even when she’s sleeping a three-hour stretch, I’m still awake, staring at the ceiling with this heavy knot in my chest.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shoulders droop]

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud parked over me. I’ll be changing her diaper and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason. Some mornings I wake up already sad, before anything’s even happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Voice cracks, eyes welling]

Yeah... a couple of times this week. Yesterday I broke down while pumping because I only got two ounces and convinced myself she’ll go hungry. I hid in the laundry room so my husband wouldn’t see, but the tears just kept coming.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[swallows hard, eyes fixed on the floor]

Once or twice… nothing planned, just—like—when she’s been crying for an hour and I can’t fix it, I’ll think, “What if I just disappeared?” I’d never leave her, I just… the thought flashes in and I feel awful for even having it.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant ~ weeks old)  
Date: [today]  
Screener: [licensed MHP]

Presenting concerns (self-report + behavioral cues)  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia: daily, present on waking.  
- Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation; even routine infant care perceived as burdensome.  
- Excessive guilt, self-blame re infant care (“failing her”).  
- Intrusive, anxious cognitions (SIDS, choking, harm befalling infant) → frequent safety-checking; no compulsive rituals reported.  
- Recurrent panic-like surges (physical, situational) without clear trigger; resolves spontaneously.  
- Overwhelm, “can’t breathe,” difficulty prioritizing tasks; occasional infant crying while parent frozen.  
- Initial insomnia (2-hr latency) with middle insomnia; sleep opportunity present.  
- Passive self-harm ideation (“What if I just disappeared?”) – denies intent or plan; protective of infant.

Pattern: Symptoms daily × ≥2 wks, onset after delivery; functional impairment evident (self-care, household tasks, social avoidance).  
Risk factors: First-time parenting, perfectionistic self-expectations, limited described support during infant distress.

Screening significance  
- Meets probable criteria for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset (PHQ-9 ≈ 18–20 range on item content).  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms meeting probable criteria for Peripartum Anxiety Disorder.  
- Passive suicidal ideation present – Safety Plan warranted.

Safety: Denies active suicidal intent; agrees to notify provider or emergency services if thoughts escalate.  
Next steps: Immediate referral to OB/Midwife for formal diagnostic evaluation, consideration of therapy (CBT/IPT), pharmacologic consult, and safety-planning; partner included if agreeable.  
Follow-up screening recommended within 1 week or sooner if symptoms intensify or self-harm thoughts become active.
